title: Reverberation is a filter you can hear
text:
ArticleFiltersAll-passes and a combThe beatCode


A synthesiser is four ideas stacked on top of each other: an oscillator that repeats, an envelope that shapes, a filter that removes, and a delay that offsets. None of them need a library. Each one here is a difference equation or a closed-form expression, and every figure below is the output of the code that implements it.

  
  One period of 200 Hz, sampled at 44.1 kHz — 220.5 samples, which is why the
  square wave changes value partway through a sample and the corners are not identical.

Sine and square are one line each. The saw is the fractional part of the running phase, \(2((ft + \phi/2\pi) \bmod 1) - 1\). The triangle is the integral of the square, which is a cumulative sum — but the integral of a square sits flat for a quarter period before the square goes positive, so each period is rotated by a quarter and the shapes line up at \(t = 0\). Both are three lines of numpy.

  
  Two envelopes: a percussive one with a 5 ms attack, and a slow pad-shaped one.

The envelope is three straight lines and a hold, which is one np.linspace per segment and no reason to be cleverer. The attack is 5 ms because anything shorter clicks. Multiplying a sine by it buys the whole difference between a tone and a note:

  
  A 220 Hz sine, and the same sine multiplied by the percussive envelope.

And multiplying by an envelope is multiplying by a signal, so in frequency it is a convolution — sidebands appear around the carrier at the envelope’s own repetition rate, and they fall off as the envelope gets more abrupt.

  
  The spectrum of the enveloped sine. The carrier is at 220 Hz and the
  sidebands sit at its neighbours, spaced by the envelope rate.



A biquad is five numerator coefficients and three denominator coefficients and a loop over the signal. scipy.signal.lfilter runs the loop; the coefficients are worth writing out by hand, because placing poles and zeros is the part that teaches anything. These are the RBJ audio EQ cookbook forms — \(\omega_0 = 2\pi f_c / f_s\), \(\alpha = \sin\omega_0 / 2Q\) — and a band-pass is the low-pass and high-pass combined into one section rather than two cascaded.

  
  The three biquads at a common 1 kHz corner, so only the shape differs. The
  band-pass uses Q = 5.

The pole-zero plot is the same object from the other side. The zeros sit on the unit circle, which is what puts notches in the response, and the poles sit just inside it at the band centre — close enough to the circle to lift the response over a narrow band, close enough to the real axis to keep it from ringing forever.

  
  Poles and zeros of the 1 kHz band-pass, in the z-plane. Zeros are crosses, poles
  are circles; the axes are the unit circle's real and imaginary parts.



An all-pass does nothing to the magnitude. It only shifts phase, and the magnitude is flat by construction: put the zeros anywhere, put the poles at their reciprocal conjugates, and np.poly gives you coefficients that cannot change the magnitude whatever you choose.

  
  A fifth-order all-pass, flat to three decimal places from DC to Nyquist.

Flat to three decimals everywhere, which is the whole point of the construction and also the reason a single all-pass is useless on its own — a filter that changes nothing is not a filter. It is only useful once you add it back to the original. The delayed version cancels at frequencies where it lands in antiphase, and the first notch falls at \(f_s / d\) — so a delay of 84 samples at 44.1 kHz puts notches every 525 Hz, which is the comb. Make the delay an all-pass instead of a pure delay and the notches spread out unevenly, which is what a phaser does and a flanger does not.

  
  A pulse train through six all-passes with delays of 40, 47, 54, 61, 68 and 75
  samples. The magnitudes are flat; the waveform is not, because the phase is not.



Kick, hat and phaser summed. The kick is a sine sliding 110 → 45 Hz over 60 ms with a saw layer for grit, under a 1 ms attack and a 150 ms decay, so it is finished before the next hit at 120 bpm. The hat is noise through a 6 kHz high-pass, gated to 50 ms, which is long enough to read as a tick and short of a snare.

  
  The mix in the time domain and in frequency. The vertical stripes are the kick
  hits at 0, 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5 s; the broadband energy above 6 kHz is the hat, offset into
  the gaps between them.


The rendered mix, 2.0 s, 88,200 samples. Kick at 0, 0.5, 1.0 and
1.5 s, hat in the gaps, phaser on top.
A last check the notebook runs on itself, which is worth keeping: convolving the pulse train with the all-pass impulse response and multiplying their FFTs give a maximum difference of 0.0886, not zero. That is not a bug. The FFT convolution is circular, so the tail of the linear convolution wraps around to the front. The two agree everywhere except where the signal is discontinuous, which is exactly where a wrapped tail lands.


rerun_notebook.py executes this notebook’s cells unmodified and captures the eleven figures. The code itself is in the notebook, not here — the page shows what it produced.

title: Choosing a model when the data is noisy
text:
ArticleRegularisationCross-validationCode


The dataset is 6,497 wines described by eleven chemical measurements — fixed and volatile acidity, citric acid, residual sugar, chlorides, free and total sulphur dioxide, density, pH, sulphates and alcohol — with a binary label for red and white. A classifier that separates them scores above 99%. That is the point of using it: the question is not whether a model fits, but where the fitting stops being honest.

  
  Left: training and test error across fifty values of the regularisation
  strength. Right: the L2 norm of the coefficient vector over the same sweep.



Training error sits at zero across four orders of magnitude of regularisation and only lifts above 0.1% once \(\lambda\) passes \(10^{-2}\). Test error is flat and close to 1.4% until roughly \(\lambda = 10^{-3}\), then descends to a minimum of 1.09% at \(\lambda = 0.222\), then climbs steeply to 2.1% at \(\lambda = 100\).
The coefficient norm falls monotonically from 229.8 to 0.904 over the same sweep. The two panels are the same story from two directions: the model does not need much freedom to separate these wines, and giving it more stops helping well before it starts to overfit the training set.
The width of the flat region matters more than the position of the minimum. Anything between about \(10^{-3}\) and \(1\) is within noise of the best result, which means the exact choice of \(\lambda\) is not a decision worth agonising over — and an honest report says so rather than quoting the argmin as if it were sharp.


Same data, different target. Alcohol is now the response and the other nine columns are the inputs. Two models — polynomial regression written from scratch, and a decision tree — compared by two-layer cross-validation: an inner loop picks the capacity, an outer loop measures generalisation error.

  folds. Positive means the tree did better. The band is the 95% confidence interval on the
  mean of the same five numbers.

Mean absolute error is 0.3536 for the polynomial and 0.3292 for the tree. Paired difference 0.0244, 95% confidence interval [0.0019, 0.0469], t = 3.01, p = 0.040 over five folds.
That interval clears zero. The tree is better, and the test to say so needed five folds to say it weakly.
Which is the interesting part. The lower bound of the interval is 0.0019 — the test is significant because the paired differences happen to cluster tight enough, not because the advantage is large. Fold 1 is a tie to three decimals and fold 3 is a rout; the interval is wide because that spread is real. Re-draw the folds and this result can move.
The hyperparameters tell a steadier story than they did on the wine target: the inner loop picked degree 3 in every single outer fold, and depth 20 in three of five. Degree 3 is where the polynomial stops gaining, which matches the sweep above — by cubic the model has as much capacity as the data supports.

title: What the outsides of a virus tell you
text:
ArticleDivergenceConvergenceClockCode


Influenza A carries eight RNA segments. Segment 4 encodes haemagglutinin, the surface glycoprotein that binds sialic acid on the host cell and mediates entry. The gene mutates fast enough that its sequence carries a record of when lineages split, and the sampling dates attached to each sequence let that record be read in years rather than in substitutions.
The dataset is 101 haemagglutinin coding sequences from GenBank — humans, birds, swine and other hosts — aligned to 1778 bp and rooted on a single H3N2 outgroup. A second dataset of 86 PB1 sequences is used as a control.

  
  The dated consensus tree from BEAST2. The scale is in years.



Node heights come from the maximum clade credibility tree with 95% highest posterior density intervals, in years before the most recent sampling date.
H5 lands at 24.84 years, interval 23.56 – 26.17, which puts the common ancestor of that clade in the 1990s — where the highly pathogenic avian lineage is first recorded, H5N1 in 1996. H1 lands at 74.42, interval 66.19 – 84.12, in the middle of the twentieth century, matching the emergence of classical swine and human H1N1. The two clades split 157.5 years back, interval 136.21 – 177.38, deeper than either, and consistent with the older literature placing the major HA subtypes several centuries back.
The widths are worth reading before the point estimates. H5 is bounded to about two and a half years; H1 is bounded to eighteen; the H1/H5 split to forty. A tighter posterior on the shallow node is what the dating model predicts — more branch lengths constrain a recent split more than an ancient one — and it is the reason the H5 date can be checked against a historical record and the split cannot.


Two independent runs per dataset. MrBayes converged cleanly: across forty tracked parameters the potential scale reduction factor ran 0.9999 to 1.0020, and effective sample sizes ran 783 to 4864, with the fifteen invariant-site proportions at 2525 to 4528.
BEAST2 did not converge to the same standard, and the gap is not evenly distributed.

  
  Transition rate r(A↔G) on the PB1 dataset, one of the parameters that mixes
  well.

On the HA log, 901 samples survive a 10% burn-in from 1001 retained. Recomputing the effective sample size on those samples separates the parameters cleanly:

  1 sits near 0.17, position 2 near 0.02, position 3 near 0.16. These are the fifteen
  proportions with effective sample sizes of 2525 to 4528, which is why they can be read off
  the figure at all.

The tree and the clock are sampled well enough to date nodes. The substitution rates are not — an effective sample size of three to seven means those posteriors are unconverged in any meaningful sense, and any statement about relative substitution rates under this model should be treated as provisional. The joint posterior inherits the worst of its components, which is why it sits at 25 while the likelihood sits at 899.
The most likely cause is the codon partition. Three partitions, each with its own substitution matrix, put the same 1778 sites behind three times as many parameters. The run was 5 million generations with 25% discarded as burn-in, and that was not enough for this parameterisation.
I also ran BEAST2 under GTR + Γ rather than GTR + I + Γ, because BEAUti flagged the invariant-sites parameter and I dropped it under time pressure without working through the consequence. That rules out a direct comparison of invariant-site estimates between the two methods, and I did not notice until both analyses were finished.

Partition 2 evolves at 4.8 times the rate of partition 1. Each mean sits more than eight standard deviations from its neighbour, so this is not posterior noise — the well-mixed clock rate is the one parameter the run can be trusted on.
That the second codon position is the fast one is the odd result. Third positions are normally closest to neutral and least constrained, and here they are three times slower than the middle position. With substitution rates at an effective sample size of three, the honest reading is that the ordering is not established by this run. It is a result that would need a longer chain, or a simpler partition, before it could be reported as anything other than a curiosity.

One of those numbers deserves saying out loud. The Robinson-Foulds distance between the two consensus trees is 172 raw, 0.9773 normalised, on 100 matching tips. Two methods given the same alignment agreed on almost none of their splits. That is a large disagreement and it is the strongest argument on this page for not quoting node ages from the BEAST2 run without the caveats above.

title: Differential expression, and what it misses
text:
ArticleThe confoundThe pathways that come backWhat it missesWhere the two disagreeCode


Ten patients from the TCGA liver hepatocellular carcinoma cohort, each contributing a tumour sample and an adjacent normal one. Twenty libraries, ~60,000 genes measured by RNA sequencing, and one question: which genes change between the two tissues.
The naive answer is thousands of them. The interesting part is what that answer leaves out.


Before any testing, the counts get a variance-stabilising transform and a PCA. The first two components should separate the conditions if the design is sound, and they do — normal samples tight on one side at 18% of variance, tumours spread across the other.
That spread is the problem. Two of the ten patients are female, and the vertical structure in the tumour cluster is partly gender. A model of condition alone is then not testing condition; it is testing condition plus whatever gender happens to correlate with.
Refitting with ~ gender + condition costs 107 genes: 5,778 significant before, 5,671 after at a 5% false discovery rate. The estimate is that it matters less than the shape of the PCA suggests, which is itself a result — a confound that is present but not dominant is different from one that isn’t there.


The 5,671 genes get ranked by their test statistic and pushed through preranked GSEA against the MSigDB biological-process collection, 15 to 500 genes per set. 865 gene sets come back significant.
They are overwhelmingly cell cycle: chromosome segregation, nuclear chromosome segregation, mitotic nuclear division, sister chromatid segregation, DNA replication, with normalised enrichment scores around 2.3 to 2.85 and adjusted p-values below 10⁻³⁴. The direction is what liver cancer biology predicts — a tumour that has lost differentiation and re-entered the cell cycle.
Against that, the top negative enrichment scores are metabolic: organic acid catabolism, small-molecule catabolism, fatty acid metabolism, at −2.6 to −3.0. Those are the processes the normal liver does and the tumour stops doing.
Two coherent stories, pointing opposite ways, from one ranked list. A leading-edge gene from the top set is NUF2, part of the NDC80 kinetochore complex that attaches chromosomes to spindle microtubules; UBE2C and NEK2 are in the same short list, both mitotic.


DESeq2 tests genes. A gene can be equally abundant in both tissues and still be doing something different — making a different isoform of the same transcript. That is differential transcript usage, and it is invisible to a gene-level test by construction.
DEXSeq asks the other question. Counts per isoform, a generalised linear model with a per-sample baseline and a per-isoform baseline, then a likelihood-ratio test of whether the condition interacts with isoform identity:
dxdSubset <- DEXSeqDataSet(
countData = lichIsoCountSubset,
sampleData = lihcMetaFull,
design= ~ sample + exon + condition:exon + gender:exon,
featureID = txInfoSubset$transcript_id,
groupID = txInfoSubset$gene_id
)

dxdSubset <- estimateSizeFactors(dxdSubset)
dxdSubset <- estimateDispersions(dxdSubset)

dxdSubset <- testForDEU(
dxdSubset,
fullModel = ~ sample + exon + condition:exon + gender:exon,
reducedModel = ~ sample + exon + gender:exon
)

dxdSubset <- estimateExonFoldChanges(dxdSubset, fitExpToVar = "condition")
dxdResult <- DEXSeqResults(dxdSubset)
Over 519 genes, 880 isoforms show significant usage shifts. The top five by adjusted p-value are KHK, UGP2, CLEC1B, FN1 and GSTZ1 — fructose metabolism, glycogen precursor synthesis, a platelet receptor, an extracellular matrix protein, and an oxidative-stress enzyme. Liver-specific metabolism, immune recognition and tissue architecture, which is the same story as the gene-level analysis told from a different angle.


Collapsing isoform results to one row per gene, then re-adjusting the false discovery rate across that new family, gives 15,312 genes tested by both methods. 1,947 are significant for isoform usage, 4,594 for overall expression, and 843 in both.
Fisher’s exact test on the 2×2 table gives an odds ratio of about 2 and p = 1.1 × 10⁻⁴⁰. Genes with differential usage are twice as likely as chance to also be differentially expressed — a real association, and nowhere near a complete one. Each method finds signals the other does not.
That gap is the point. Running the same GSEA on both gene rankings and plotting the normalised enrichment scores against each other shows the answer at pathway level:



Spearman correlation of NES
−0.082


significant in both
a minority


pathways significant only in one
the majority



A negative correlation between the two rankings means that for a great many pathways, the gene-level analysis and the isoform-level analysis do not merely disagree on magnitude — they disagree on direction. Not on the same pathways, but not in the same direction.
The conservative reading is that isoform-level testing is noisier and this is what noise looks like. The reading I would defend is narrower: at the gene level, 5,671 genes separate tumour from normal, and that number is an upper bound on how much of the biology the analysis captured. The rest is in how the transcripts are put together.

# Step 2: Filter the virtual pulldown to remove "sticky" hub proteins
# Function takes a subgraph, the full parent graph, and a cutoff threshold.
filter_virtual_pulldown <- function(subGraph, parentGraph, cutoff) {
  
  # --- Check that both graphs have vertex names (proteins identified by name) ---
  if (is.null(V(subGraph)$name) || is.null(V(parentGraph)$name))
    stop("Both graphs must have vertex 'name' attributes.")
  
  # --- Mode: "all" ensures degrees are calculated without direction ---
  mode <- "all"
  
  # --- Extract node names from the subgraph ---
  vn <- V(subGraph)$name
  
  # --- Degree in the full graph: total number of connections each node has globally ---
  deg_full <- degree(parentGraph, v = vn, mode = mode)
  
  # --- Degree in the subgraph: number of connections each node has inside the pulldown ---
  deg_internal <- degree(subGraph, mode = mode)
  
  # --- Combine results into a data frame for each node ---
  res <- data.frame(
    node          = vn,
    deg_internal  = deg_internal,
    deg_full      = deg_full,
    # Fraction of a node’s total connections that lie within this pulldown
    frac_internal = ifelse(deg_full > 0, deg_internal / deg_full, NA_real_),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  
  # --- Keep only nodes that meet the cutoff for internal fraction ---
  nodes_to_keep <- res$node[!is.na(res$frac_internal) & res$frac_internal >= cutoff]
  
  # --- Build a new subgraph using only the kept nodes ---
  filteredSubGraph <- induced_subgraph(subGraph, vids = V(subGraph)[name %in% nodes_to_keep])
  
  # --- Add the fraction value as a vertex attribute (for later inspection) ---
  V(filteredSubGraph)$frac_internal <- res$frac_internal[match(V(filteredSubGraph)$name, res$node)]
  
  # --- Return the filtered network ---
  filteredSubGraph
}

  expected   <- (res$size / length(universe)) * length(target)
  enrichment <- res$overlap / expected
  out <- cbind(res, expected, enrichment)
  out[order(res$padj, res$pval), ]
}

# GOAL:
# Collapse isoform-level DEXSeq results to one row per gene by:
#   (a) picking the most significant isoform per gene (smallest RAW p-value),
#   (b) then recomputing FDR across genes (new hypothesis family).
# WHY:
#   The original DEXSeq 'padj' adjusts across ALL isoforms/features. After collapsing to
#   one p-value per gene, that 'padj' is no longer valid; we must re-adjust at the gene level.

dexseqResultGene <-
  dexseqResult %>%
  as.data.frame() %>%        # Convert S4 results object to a plain data.frame
  as_tibble() %>%            # and then to a tibble for friendly dplyr usage

  # 1) Keep only tested features (rows where the test statistic exists).
  #    NAs often arise from zero counts, filtering, or non-convergence.
  filter(!is.na(stat)) %>%

  # 2) Select and rename columns we need downstream.
  #    - groupID   : gene identifier as supplied when building the DEXSeqDataSet (here: Ensembl gene id)
  #    - featureID : feature identifier (here: transcript/isoform id, because we set featureID = transcript_id)
  #    - stat      : test statistic for the DEU test on this feature
  #    - log2fold_Primary_Tumor_Solid_Tissue_Normal : feature-level log2FC for the 'condition' contrast
  #    - pvalue    : RAW p-value for this feature (used to pick per-gene "best" isoform)
  #    - padj      : feature-level FDR across ALL features (not valid after collapsing to genes)
  dplyr::select(
    gene_id    = groupID,
    isoform_id = featureID,
    stat,
    log2FC     = log2fold_Primary_Tumor_Solid_Tissue_Normal,
    pvalue,
    padj
  ) %>%

  # 3) Group by gene to operate within each gene's set of isoforms/features.
  group_by(gene_id) %>%

  # 4) Within each gene, keep the single isoform with the smallest RAW p-value.
  #    WHY raw p (not feature-level padj)? Because we are about to define a NEW testing family
  #    (one p per gene) and must feed those raw p-values into a fresh multiple-testing correction.
  slice_min(
    order_by = pvalue,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE  # if two isoforms tie exactly, pick one arbitrarily (see tie-breaking alternative below)
  ) %>%

  # 5) Ungroup so the next mutate acts on the entire tibble.
  ungroup() %>%

  # 6) Recompute FDR across genes (new hypothesis family = "one p per gene").
  #    This is statistically correct and typically more powerful (fewer tests than "all isoforms").
  #    Note: method = "fdr" is an alias for Benjamini–Hochberg ("BH").
  mutate(padj = p.adjust(pvalue, method = "fdr"))

# • Low coverage: Very lowly expressed features can yield noisy min-p selections; consider prefiltering by coverage/baseMean if you see suspicious genes.

###############################################
# STEP 1 — Choose a cutoff for "significant"
###############################################

# Here we decide that any adjusted p-value (padj) smaller than 0.05
# means that the gene is significantly different.
# 0.05 is a common threshold — it represents a 5% false discovery rate.
alpha <- 0.05

###############################################
# STEP 2 — (Optional) Clean gene IDs
###############################################

# Sometimes gene IDs have version numbers at the end (like ENSG000001234.12).
# DESeq2 and DEXSeq might handle these differently, so we make sure both use the same format.
# This function removes everything after a dot and the digits following it.
strip_ver <- function(x) sub("\\.\\d+$", "", x)

###############################################
# STEP 3 — Prepare the DEXSeq results
###############################################

# The dexseqResultGene table already has one row per gene (after collapsing isoforms).
# We add a TRUE/FALSE column saying whether each gene is significant.

dex_gene <- dexseqResultGene %>%
  mutate(
    gene_id = strip_ver(gene_id),   # make sure gene IDs are version-free and comparable
    dex_padj = padj,                # keep padj for clarity
    dex_sig  = !is.na(padj) & padj < alpha  # TRUE if padj < 0.05 and not missing
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(gene_id, dex_padj, dex_sig) # keep only relevant columns
dex_gene

###############################################
# STEP 4 — Prepare the DESeq2 results
###############################################

# Do exactly the same thing for the DESeq2 gene-level results.
# Again, add a TRUE/FALSE flag for significance.

deseq_gene <- deseq2Results %>%
  mutate(
    gene_id = strip_ver(gene_id),   # remove version suffix
    deseq_padj = padj,              # keep padj column
    deseq_sig  = !is.na(padj) & padj < alpha  # mark significant genes
  ) %>%
  dplyr::select(gene_id, deseq_padj, deseq_sig)
deseq_gene

###############################################
# STEP 5 — Define the universe of comparable genes
###############################################

# Both DEXSeq and DESeq2 may have tested slightly different sets of genes.
# We only want to compare the ones that appear in BOTH.
# This gives us the "gene universe" for the overlap test.
univ <- intersect(dex_gene$gene_id, deseq_gene$gene_id)

# Sanity check: how many genes are shared between the two analyses?
length(univ)

###############################################
# STEP 6 — Combine both results side-by-side
###############################################

# Merge the two tables by gene_id, so that each gene now has:
# - its DEXSeq significance (dex_sig)
# - its DESeq2 significance (deseq_sig)

both <- dex_gene %>%
  filter(gene_id %in% univ) %>%      # keep only shared genes
  inner_join(deseq_gene, by = "gene_id")  # join DESeq2 results by gene_id

# Quick look to make sure it worked
head(both)

###############################################
# STEP 7 — Count overlaps (the "both TRUE" genes)
###############################################

# This is the number of genes significant in both methods.
n_overlap <- sum(both$dex_sig & both$deseq_sig)

# Also useful to know total counts for context.
n_dex_sig   <- sum(both$dex_sig)
n_deseq_sig <- sum(both$deseq_sig)
n_universe  <- nrow(both)

# Print them
cat("Universe:", n_universe, "\n")
cat("DEXSeq significant:", n_dex_sig, "\n")
cat("DESeq2 significant:", n_deseq_sig, "\n")
cat("Overlap:", n_overlap, "\n")


###############################################
# STEP 8 — Build the 2×2 contingency table
###############################################

# This table shows every possible combination:
# - Neither method found it
# - Only DESeq2 found it
# - Only DEXSeq found it
# - Both found it

contig_tab <- table(DEXSeq = both$dex_sig, DESeq2 = both$deseq_sig)
contig_tab

###############################################
# STEP 9 — Run Fisher’s exact test (ORA)
###############################################

# Fisher’s Exact Test asks:
# "Is the overlap (TRUE + TRUE) larger than we would expect by random chance?"

ft <- fisher.test(contig_tab, alternative = "greater")

# Print the result
ft

  p_value      = ft$p.value
)

# GOAL
# Compare pathway-level enrichment between DESeq2 (gene-level)
# and DEXSeq (isoform-usage) by plotting their NES scores
# against each other. Color points by which analysis called
# the pathway significant (DEXSeq only, DESeq2 only, Both, None).
#
# INPUTS WE ALREADY HAVE:
#   fg_deseq : fgseaMultilevel() result for DESeq2 stats
#   fg_dex   : fgseaMultilevel() result for DEXSeq  stats
#   alpha    : significance cutoff (e.g., 0.05)
#
# OUTPUT:
#   1) A merged data.frame `cmp` with NES + padj from both analyses
#   2) A scatterplot NES(DESeq2) vs NES(DEXSeq) colored by significance class
############################################################

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

# 1) Keep just the columns we need from each fgsea result and rename them
#    so they won't collide when we join the two tables later.
#    - pathway : the gene set name (join key)
#    - NES     : normalized enrichment score (effect size; up/down and magnitude)
#    - padj    : FDR-adjusted p-value for the gene set (significance)
#
#    `transmute()` creates a new data.frame with only the columns we list.
#    We also rename NES/padj to method-specific names (NES_de/padj_de, NES_dx/padj_dx).
de_df <- fg_deseq %>%
  transmute(
    pathway,
    NES_de  = NES,
    padj_de = padj
  )

dx_df <- fg_dex %>%
  transmute(
    pathway,
    NES_dx  = NES,
    padj_dx = padj
  )

# 2) Merge (inner join) on 'pathway' so we keep only gene sets present in BOTH
#    results. This is necessary because we want to plot NES_de vs NES_dx for
#    the same pathway on each row.
#
#    After the join, add a "sig_cat" (significance category) column:
#      - "Both"         : padj < alpha in DESeq2 AND in DEXSeq
#      - "DESeq2 only"  : padj < alpha in DESeq2, but not in DEXSeq
#      - "DEXSeq only"  : padj < alpha in DEXSeq, but not in DESeq2
#      - "None"         : padj >= alpha in both
#
#    Finally, we make sig_cat an ordered factor so the legend uses a sensible order.
cmp <- inner_join(de_df, dx_df, by = "pathway") %>%
  # fgsea can leave a few rows with NA NES/padj (e.g., "unbalanced" sets).
  # Drop NAs so plotting/statistics don't choke.
  filter(!is.na(NES_de), !is.na(NES_dx), !is.na(padj_de), !is.na(padj_dx)) %>%
  mutate(
    sig_cat = case_when(
      padj_de < alpha & padj_dx < alpha ~ "Both",
      padj_de < alpha & padj_dx >= alpha ~ "DESeq2 only",
      padj_de >= alpha & padj_dx < alpha ~ "DEXSeq only",
      TRUE ~ "None"
    ),
    sig_cat = factor(sig_cat, levels = c("Both", "DESeq2 only", "DEXSeq only", "None"))
  )

# 3) (Optional but useful) Compute correlations so we can report a number.
#    Spearman = monotonic rank correlation (robust to outliers, scale-free).
#    Pearson  = linear correlation.
spearman_cor <- cor(cmp$NES_de, cmp$NES_dx, method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs")
pearson_cor  <- cor(cmp$NES_de, cmp$NES_dx, method = "pearson",  use = "complete.obs")

# 4) Make the scatterplot:
#    - x = DESeq2 NES; y = DEXSeq NES
#    - color by significance category
#    - add a linear trend line (geom_smooth with method = "lm") WITHOUT a gray CI ribbon
#      to avoid clutter; the line just indicates the direction/strength visually.
p <- ggplot(cmp, aes(x = NES_de, y = NES_dx, color = sig_cat)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +                 # points for each pathway
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +  # dashed trend line (no CI)
  labs(
    x = "NES (DESeq2 fgsea)",               # clear axis labels
    y = "NES (DEXSeq fgsea)",
    color = "Significance",
    title = "NES comparison: DESeq2 vs DEXSeq (fgseaMultilevel)",
    subtitle = paste0("Spearman r = ", round(spearman_cor, 3),
                      " | Pearson r = ", round(pearson_cor, 3),
                      " | alpha = ", alpha)
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# 5) Print the plot
p
